common_name: Granddaddy's Okra (Texas Eubanks Family Heirloom Okra)

planting.note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed once soil has warmed above 65F; Granddaddy's traces to four generations of the Eubanks family of Whitney, Texas, and was later found growing in the garden of a Texas Organic Farmers and Gardeners Association founder before Seed Savers Exchange and Sow True Seed helped preserve and distribute it.

directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in warm, well-drained soil in full sun once the ground has heated up after the last frost. Granddaddy's produces long, slender pods with good flavor that stay tender past the size where many other okra turn fibrous, though picking under 6 inches still gives the best eating quality. Pick every two to three days through the heat of summer to keep the vigorous, heavily branched plants setting new pods, and expect production to hold up well even under typical late-season disease pressure. This is a true multigenerational family heirloom rather than a commercial release, so seed stock traces directly back to the Eubanks family line.
sources: Texas Organic Farmers and Gardeners Association

planting.note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed once soil is warm; this heirloom moved from DeQuincy, Louisiana to Lawrence Langston of Dripping Springs, Texas, who maintained and eventually shared it through Seed Savers Exchange.

directions: Direct sow an inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Langston Longhorn is an old-fashioned heavily branched okra with green stems showing red blushing, capable of reaching well above standard okra height in a long warm season. The slender, pale yellow-green pods carry spines near the cap, so gloves are a good idea at harvest, and pods are best picked under 4 inches for tenderness since this variety fibers up quickly past that size. Pick frequently — ideally daily once plants hit stride — to sustain the heavy, continuous pod set this variety is known for.
sources: Sow True Seed — Langston Longhorn Okra

common_name: Whidby White Okra (Georgia Heirloom Pale Spineless Okra)

planting.note: Direct sow once frost danger has fully passed and soil has warmed; Whidby White was donated to Seed Savers Exchange in the mid-1980s by a Georgia family that had kept it since the mid-1800s, then nearly vanished before the Utopian Seed Project and regional seed growers revived it around 2018.

directions: Direct sow an inch deep in full sun in warm, well-drained soil; Whidby White is a rare Southern heirloom grown for its short, pale, deeply ridged pods that are naturally spineless and easy to handle at harvest. The pale coloring sets it visibly apart from the standard green okra most Gulf South gardeners are used to, and the short pod length means it needs closer watching to catch pods at their most tender. This variety was nearly lost entirely before community seed-saving efforts restored it, so it is a genuine rescue heirloom rather than a long-available commercial strain.
sources: Sow True Seed — Whidby White Okra

common_name: Sea Island Red Okra (Gullah Geechee Heirloom Okra)

planting.note: Direct sow once soil is warm and frost danger has passed; this okra traces to Gullah Geechee seed-keeping on Sapelo Island, Georgia, associated with matriarch Cornelia Bailey and later maintained through University of Georgia's research and education program at Wormsloe.

directions: Direct sow an inch deep in full sun in warm, fertile soil; Sea Island Red is a moderately branching okra with striking dark red stems and velvety, lightly ridged red pods that run 6 to 8 inches at full size. It carries deep cultural significance as a Gullah Geechee coastal heirloom and remains rare in commercial seed trade, so growing it out and saving seed helps keep the line going. Harvest regularly at 3-4 inches for the most tender pods, and expect the ornamental dark coloring of stems and pods to make this a standout plant in the summer vegetable bed.
sources: Sow True Seed — Sea Island Red Okra
University of Georgia Center for Research and Education at Wormsloe

common_name: Bradford Family Okra (South Carolina Heirloom Okra)

planting.note: Scarify seed and direct sow an inch deep after last frost once soil is reliably warm; Bradford Family has been grown by the Bradford family of Sumter, South Carolina since the 1920s and was reintroduced to chefs by Nat Bradford starting in 2017.

directions: Nick or scarify the hard seed coat before direct sowing an inch deep in full sun; Bradford Family is unusual among okra for staying tender even at 6 to 8 inches long, with pod tips that snap cleanly rather than turning fibrous at that size. The pods are notably sweet and large enough to stuff, and the plump seeds inside have drawn comparisons to caviar from chefs who have cooked with this once nearly-forgotten Lowcountry heirloom. Harvest every two to three days during peak summer production to keep plants setting new flowers, and expect strong continuous yields in Gulf South heat once plants are established.
sources: Sow True Seed — Bradford Family Okra
Anson Mills / Nat Bradford seed history accounts

planting.note: Direct sow (or transplant for an earlier start) after frost danger has passed once soil is warm; Jambalaya 2.0 is a newer F1 hybrid update to the original compact Jambalaya okra, sold by Johnny's Selected Seeds for its earlier maturity and more uniform pod set.

directions: Direct sow an inch deep in warm, fertile soil in full sun, or start indoors for an earlier harvest in cooler springs; Jambalaya 2.0 is a compact, early F1 hybrid producing highly uniform, dark green pods with five distinct ridges. Harvest at 3-4 inches for tenderness, checking plants every couple of days once production ramps up, since this hybrid's uniform pod set means a flush of pods can mature together. The large showy flowers are edible and, combined with the plant's compact size, make it a good option for containers and small raised beds where a shorter okra plant is wanted without giving up yield.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Jambalaya 2.0 F1 Okra
